groups.label: Rising & Falling Intonation
groups.definition: Pitch movement in statements and questions
rules: Yes/No questions end with rising intonation ↗.
Wh- questions and statements end with falling intonation ↘.

groups.label: Connected Speech & Linking
rules: Final consonants link smoothly to initial vowels of the next word.
Words flow together in continuous speech streams.

groups.label: Question Tag Intonation
groups.definition: Pitch variations determining whether a question tag asks or confirms
rules: Falling intonation ↘ on a question tag indicates checking agreement rather than asking a genuine question.
Rising intonation ↗ on a question tag indicates a genuine request for information.

examples.t: You haven't seen my keys, have you? ↗
examples.m: Rising tag intonation asking a real question

groups.label: Choice & Polite Request Intonation
groups.definition: Intonation contours in alternative questions and courteous requests
rules: In choice questions with 'or', pitch rises on the first option and falls on the final option ↗↘.
Polite requests use a rising or fall-rising intonation to sound open and friendly rather than demanding.

examples.t: Would you like tea ↗ or coffee ↘?
examples.m: Rising on first option, falling on final choice

examples.t: Could you open the door, please? ↗

groups.label: Contrastive & Tonic Intonation
groups.definition: Shifting nucleus stress and pitch contour to highlight specific information or express nuance
rules: Moving tonic stress to non-standard words shifts contrastive focus to correct information or highlight alternatives.
Fall-rise intonation ↘↗ expresses reservation, uncertainty, or polite disagreement.

examples.t: I wanted RED shoes, not black. 🎯
examples.m: Contrastive stress on the color adjective
Fall-rise pitch expressing hesitation or qualification

groups.label: Thought Groups & Chunking
groups.definition: Dividing speech into meaningful intonation units (thought groups) and lower pitch for parentheticals
rules: Long sentences are broken into thought groups (intonavial phrases), with each group having its own pitch movement and pause.
Parenthetical remarks, commentary, or non-defining clauses are spoken at a lower pitch and faster tempo.

examples.t: If you need help ↗ / just give me a call ↘.
examples.m: Thought group pause between subordinate and main clause

examples.t: My sister, (who lives in Paris), ↘ is visiting today.
examples.m: Lower pitch for non-defining relative clause
